title: For all and there exists
objectives: Write statements with “for all” and “there exists”, and see why their order matters.

screens.title: Every trader, some day
screens.prose: Four traders' profit and loss, in £, over one week. Claim A: **every trader made more than £100 on some day**.
screens.question: Show claim A is true: tap one day for each trader on which they made more than £100.

hints.text: Take the traders one row at a time.
In each row, look for a number above 100.
T1 on Wed (150), T2 on Thu (210), T3 on Thu (130), T4 on Tue (110).

feedback.correct: One cell per trader: T1 Wed, T2 Thu, T3 Thu, T4 Tue.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. In each row, find the one number above 100.

byKey.all-profits: You tapped every profit. The claim needs more than £100, and one such day per trader.
byKey.r4c4: T4 made £95 on Thursday. That is a profit, but not more than £100.
byKey.r3c3: T3 made £90 on Wednesday, not more than £100.
byKey.r1c3: Keep T1's Wednesday: £150 is the day that shows the claim for T1.
byKey.r4c2: T4 needs a day too. Tuesday's £110 is the only one above £100.

explain.text: Each trader has a day above £100, so claim A is true. Notice the days differ: T1 needs Wednesday, T4 needs Tuesday.

canvas.caption: A day above £100 for each trader

screens.title: Is there one day for everyone?
screens.prose: Claim B: **there is a day on which every trader made more than £100**. Thursday looks promising: T2 made £210 and T3 made £130.
screens.question: Tap one cell that shows “every trader made more than £100 on Thursday” is false.

hints.text: Read down the Thursday column.
Two traders did not clear £100 on Thursday.
T1 lost £20 on Thursday. T4's £95 also falls short.

feedback.correct: One trader below £100 is enough to sink Thursday.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find a Thursday value that is £100 or less.

byKey.r2c4: T2 made £210 on Thursday, which is over £100.
byKey.r3c4: T3 made £130 on Thursday, which is over £100.
byKey.too-many: One cell is enough. A single trader below £100 already breaks the claim for Thursday.
byKey.r1c3: That cell is Wednesday. The question is about the Thursday column.

explain.text: T1's −£20 breaks the claim for Thursday, and so does T4's £95. One counterexample is enough.

canvas.caption: Thursday fails for T1 and T4

screens.title: For all, there exists
screens.prose: We write $\forall$ for “for every” and $\exists$ for “there exists”. Let $P(t, d)$ mean “trader $t$ made more than £100 on day $d$”. The day you tapped for each trader is a **witness**. The traders and the days are each variable's **domain**.
screens.question: Build claim A from the chips. Some chips are not needed.

hints.text: Claim A starts “every trader”.
After “every trader” comes “made more than £100 on some day”.
$\forall$ trader $t$, $\exists$ day $d$, $P(t, d)$.

feedback.correct: $\forall t\ \exists d\ P(t, d)$: for every trader there is a day.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read claim A aloud and put the chips in that order.

byKey.ex_d: You put “there exists a day” first. That is claim B's order: one day for all traders.
byKey.fa_d: “For every day” would ask for a profit above £100 on all five days.
byKey.ex_t: “There exists a trader” would ask for only one trader.
byKey.fa_t: Start with “for every trader”, then the day.

explain.text: Claim A is $\forall t\ \exists d\ P(t, d)$. The $\exists d$ comes after $\forall t$, so each trader may have their own witness day.

screens.title: The domain matters
screens.prose: $\mathbb{R}$ is the real numbers and $\mathbb{Z}$ the integers, the whole numbers with their negatives. $x \in \mathbb{R}$ reads “$x$ is in $\mathbb{R}$”.
screens.question: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: $\forall x \in \mathbb{R},\ x^2 \ge 0$
$\exists x \in \mathbb{R},\ x^2 = 2$
$\exists x \in \mathbb{Z},\ x^2 = 2$
options.why: You allowed a non-integer witness. $1^2 = 1$ and $2^2 = 4$, so no integer squares to 2.

options.text: $\forall x \in \mathbb{R},\ x^2 > 0$
options.why: You missed $x = 0$. There $x^2 = 0$, which is not greater than 0.

hints.text: A $\forall$ claim fails if one value breaks it. An $\exists$ claim needs one witness.
Try $x = 0$ in the claims about every real number.
$x^2 \ge 0$ holds for every real, but $0^2 > 0$ fails. $\sqrt{2}$ is a real witness, yet no integer squares to 2.

feedback.correct: Right. The same claim can be true over $\mathbb{R}$ and false over $\mathbb{Z}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test each $\forall$ claim at 0 and look for a witness for each $\exists$ claim.

byKey.introot: You kept the integer version. $\sqrt{2}$ lies between 1 and 2, so no integer works.
byKey.strict: You kept $x^2 > 0$. At $x = 0$ it fails, so it is not true for every real.
byKey.sq: You left out $x^2 \ge 0$. A square is never negative, so it holds for every real.
byKey.root: You left out the real square root. $x = \sqrt{2}$ is a witness.

explain.text: $\sqrt{2}$ is a witness over $\mathbb{R}$, but it is not an integer. So changing the domain changed the truth value. The value $x = 0$ breaks $x^2 > 0$.

screens.title: Swap the order
screens.prose: Over the integers, compare two claims. First: $\forall x\ \exists y,\ y > x$. Second: $\exists y\ \forall x,\ y > x$. The line shows one $x$ and a $y$ for it.
screens.question: Which claims are true?

options.text: Only the first
Both
options.why: You read them as the same claim. The second needs one $y$ bigger than every integer, and $y + 1$ beats it.

options.text: Only the second
options.why: You chose the stronger claim. If one $y$ beat every $x$, it would have to beat $x = y$ itself.

options.text: Neither
options.why: The first is true: for any $x$, the witness $y = x + 1$ works.

hints.text: In the first claim, $y$ may depend on $x$. In the second, one $y$ must serve every $x$.
For the first, try $y = x + 1$.
No single integer is larger than every integer, since $y + 1$ would beat it. So only the first holds.

feedback.correct: Only the first. Each $x$ gets its own $y$, but no single $y$ beats them all.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Decide whether $y$ may change with $x$ in each claim.

byKey.both: You treated the two orders as one claim. Swapping $\forall$ and $\exists$ changes what is claimed.

explain.text: In $\forall x\ \exists y$, the witness $y = x + 1$ is chosen after $x$. In $\exists y\ \forall x$, one $y$ must beat every integer, including $y$ itself. There is no largest integer, so the second is false.

screens.title: A rule you have met
screens.prose: In Functions you met the rule for a function: **for every input there is exactly one output**. That is a $\forall$ followed by an $\exists$. This table pairs inputs with outputs.
screens.question: Is the table a function, and why?

options.text: No. Input 2 has two outputs, so “exactly one” fails
No. Inputs 1 and 3 share the output 5
options.why: Several inputs may share an output. The rule limits outputs per input, not inputs per output.

options.text: Yes. Every input has an output
options.why: You checked “there is an output” but not “exactly one”. Input 2 has two.

options.text: No. Input 4 has no output
options.why: 4 is not in the domain here. The domain is the inputs 1, 2 and 3.

hints.text: Check each input in turn. How many outputs does it have?
Look at the rows for input 2.
Input 2 has outputs 7 and 9. “Exactly one” fails there.

feedback.correct: Right. The $\exists$ part asks for exactly one output, and input 2 has two.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the outputs of each input.

byKey.shared: You objected to a shared output. Many inputs may share one output; one input may not have two.

explain.text: The rule is $\forall x\ \exists$ exactly one output. Inputs 1 and 3 have one each, but input 2 has two. So the table is not a function.

screens.title: Claim B
screens.prose: Back to the traders. Claim A, $\forall t\ \exists d\ P(t, d)$, is true. Claim B is $\exists d\ \forall t\ P(t, d)$: **there is a day on which every trader made more than £100**.
screens.question: Is claim B true?

options.text: No. On every day, some trader made £100 or less
Yes. Every trader had a day above £100
options.why: You used claim A's witnesses. Claim B needs one day for all four traders at once, and the shaded days differ.

options.text: Yes. Thursday works
options.why: Thursday fails: T1 lost £20 and T4 made £95.

options.text: We cannot tell from the table
options.why: The table has every day and every trader. Check each column for a value of £100 or less.

hints.text: Claim B needs one column where all four values are above 100.
Each column has at most two values above 100.
Mon, Tue, Wed and Fri each have a value of 100 or less, and so does Thu.

feedback.correct: Right. No column clears £100 for all four traders, so B is false.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for one column with every value above 100.

byKey.swap: You read B as A. Swapping $\forall$ and $\exists$ asks for one day shared by every trader, and no such day exists.

explain.text: Claim A lets each trader pick a day; claim B needs one shared day. Every column has a value of £100 or less, so B is false. The order of $\forall$ and $\exists$ changed the claim.

canvas.caption: A value of £100 or less in every column

screens.title: No trades at all
screens.prose: On a market holiday the desk made no trades. The risk log reads: **every trade today breached its limit**.
screens.question: Is the log's sentence true?

options.text: True. There is no trade that fails to breach
False. No trade breached anything
options.why: You looked for a breach. A $\forall$ claim fails only if some trade does not breach, and there is no trade at all.

options.text: It is not a statement on a day with no trades
options.why: It is a statement; it is just true for an odd reason.

options.text: True and false at once
options.why: A statement is never both. Check whether any trade breaks the claim.

hints.text: To show a $\forall$ claim false, you need one trade that does not breach.
Is there any trade to point to?
With no trades there is no counterexample, so the claim is true. It is vacuously true, as in If, then.

feedback.correct: True, vacuously. Over an empty domain every $\forall$ claim is true.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what would make the claim false.

byKey.false: You read it as “some trade breached”. That $\exists$ claim is false today, but the $\forall$ claim is true.

explain.text: A $\forall$ claim is false only if a counterexample exists. With no trades there is none, so the claim is true. By the same logic, every $\exists$ claim over no trades is false.

screens.title: Order matters
screens.prose:
Claim A allowed a different witness for each trader. Claim B demanded one witness for everyone:

$$\exists d\ \forall t\ P(t, d) \Rightarrow \forall t\ \exists d\ P(t, d)$$

The arrow does not run the other way, as the traders showed.
screens.question: Why does B imply A?

options.text: B's one day serves as every trader's witness
A and B are the same claim
options.why: The traders' table makes A true and B false, so they are different claims.

options.text: It does not: A implies B instead
options.why: A is true and B false in the traders' table, so A cannot imply B.

options.text: Because there are more days than traders
options.why: The counts do not matter. One shared day works for every trader, however many there are.

feedback.correct: Right. If one day works for everyone, each trader can use that day.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Suppose B is true and find a witness for each trader.

byKey.same: You treated the orders as interchangeable. The traders' table separates them.

explain.text: If B holds with day $d_0$, then every trader made more than £100 on $d_0$. So each trader has a witness, and A holds. The traders' table shows A can hold without B.

screens.title: Hedging a book
screens.prose: Three possible hedges for a bond book, against four overnight scenarios. A tick means the hedge protects the book in that scenario. The desk cannot trade overnight, so it must pick one hedge tonight.
screens.question: Which claim does the desk need, and is it true here?

options.text: There is one hedge that protects in every scenario. False here
For every scenario there is a hedge that protects. True here, so the desk is safe
options.why: That claim lets the desk switch hedges after the news. It is true here, but this desk cannot switch overnight.

options.text: There is one hedge that protects in every scenario. True here: H1
options.why: H1 fails if rates fall. Each hedge has a cross somewhere.

options.text: For every scenario there is a hedge that protects. False here
options.why: Every column has a tick, so this claim is true. It is just not the one the desk needs.

hints.text: The desk must choose before the scenario is known. Which quantifier comes first?
“There is one hedge” comes first, then “for every scenario”.
That needs a row of four ticks. Each row has a cross.

feedback.correct: Right. The desk needs $\exists$ hedge $\forall$ scenario, and no row is all ticks.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Decide whether the hedge is chosen before or after the scenario.

byKey.dyn-t: You picked $\forall$ scenario $\exists$ hedge. It allows a new hedge for each scenario, which needs trading overnight.

explain.text: A static hedge needs $\exists h\ \forall s$: one row of ticks. Every row has a cross, so no single hedge works. The weaker $\forall s\ \exists h$ is true, but only a desk that can rebalance can use it.

ideas: $\forall x\ P(x)$ says every value in the domain works; one counterexample breaks it. $\exists x\ P(x)$ needs one witness.
The domain matters: $\exists x,\ x^2 = 2$ is true over $\mathbb{R}$ and false over $\mathbb{Z}$. Over an empty domain, $\forall$ claims are true and $\exists$ claims false.
Order matters: $\exists y\ \forall x$ implies $\forall x\ \exists y$, but not the other way round.

formula.name: Order of quantifiers
formula.tex: \exists y\ \forall x\ P(x, y) \Rightarrow \forall x\ \exists y\ P(x, y)
formula.note: In $\forall x\ \exists y$ the witness $y$ may depend on $x$.

summary.trap: “Every trader had a good day” does not give “there was a day good for every trader”.

quiz.prose: Each statement is about the integers $\mathbb{Z}$.
quiz.question: Which are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: $\forall n \in \mathbb{Z},\ n^2 \ge n$
$\exists n \in \mathbb{Z},\ 2n = 7$
options.why: You allowed $n = 3.5$. It is not an integer, and $2n$ is always even.

options.text: $\forall n \in \mathbb{Z}\ \exists m \in \mathbb{Z},\ m = 2n$
$\exists m \in \mathbb{Z}\ \forall n \in \mathbb{Z},\ m = 2n$
options.why: You swapped the order. One fixed $m$ cannot be double every integer at once.

feedback.correct: Right. $n^2 \ge n$ holds for every integer, and each $n$ has its own double.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test each claim with small integers, including 0 and negatives.

explain.text: For $n \le 0$, $n^2 \ge 0 \ge n$; for $n \ge 1$, $n^2 = n \times n \ge n$. Each $n$ has the witness $m = 2n$, but no single $m$ works for every $n$.

options.why: You took the 9 itself. $9^2 = 81$.

options.text: None: an $\exists$ claim needs every $x$
options.why: An $\exists$ claim needs only one value that works.

feedback.correct: Right. $3^2 = 9$, and $-3$ would do as well.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A witness is one value that makes the sentence true.

explain.text: $3^2 = 9$, so 3 is a witness and the claim is true. $-3$ is another witness; one is enough.

quiz.prose: The desk holds no options at all. Consider: **there is an option the desk holds that expires this week**.
quiz.question: Is the sentence true?

options.text: False. There is no option to be a witness
True, vacuously, like an empty $\forall$ claim
options.why: You carried the empty-domain rule over to $\exists$. An $\exists$ claim needs a witness, and there is none.

options.text: It is not a statement
options.why: It is a statement, and it is false.

options.text: We cannot tell without the expiry dates
options.why: With no options there are no dates to check. No witness can exist.

feedback.correct: Right. Over an empty domain every $\exists$ claim is false.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. An $\exists$ claim needs one witness.

explain.text: An $\exists$ claim is true only if a witness exists. The desk holds no options, so there is none and the claim is false.

quiz.prose: S: **there is a day on which every stock in the fund rose**. W: **every stock in the fund rose on some day**.
quiz.question: Which is right?

options.text: If S is true, W must be true
If W is true, S must be true
options.why: You ran the arrow backwards. Each stock may have risen on a different day.

options.text: S and W say the same thing
options.why: They differ: W allows a different day for each stock.

options.text: Neither ever follows from the other
options.why: S gives W: the shared day serves every stock.

feedback.correct: Right. One shared day works as every stock's witness.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write each as $\exists$ and $\forall$ in order.

explain.text: S is $\exists d\ \forall s$ and W is $\forall s\ \exists d$. The shared day in S is a witness for each stock in W. The reverse can fail.
